title: Built to Deliver the Answer, Not to Train the Model
gist: VSORA argues AI inference, now most data-center AI workloads, is limited by memory movement rather than peak FLOPS, and presents a compiler-scheduled, chiplet-based architecture (Jotunn8, Tyr) to address it. Performance and utilization claims are company-sourced and unverified.

insights.claim: Industry estimates now place inference at most data-center AI workloads, after a decade of hardware focus on training.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Capex and silicon demand are shifting toward inference-optimized hardware; favors architectures beyond training GPUs.

insights.claim: Peak FLOPS no longer adequately measures inference processors; what matters is useful throughput within limits on latency, power, memory and cost.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Evaluate accelerators on delivered throughput under constraints, not spec-sheet peaks.
insights.quote: A more useful measure is how much work a processor completes while meeting real limits on latency, power, memory, and cost.

insights.claim: Hardware designed mainly for training may be poorly suited to delivering answers, since inference demands more data movement, handles fast-changing workloads and operates under strict latency limits.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Opens room for inference-specific challengers to incumbent GPU platforms.

insights.claim: Inference runs continuously and serves millions of requests over a model's deployed life, so small inefficiencies repeat on every request and hardware utilization, energy efficiency and cost per output directly drive operating expense.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Inference economics reward efficiency; operating cost, not just capex, drives accelerator choice.

insights.claim: Inference can often use lower precision such as INT8, FP8, INT4 or FP4 to cut model size, memory traffic and energy, provided accuracy stays acceptable.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Low-precision support is a key accelerator feature for inference.

insights.claim: Predictable timing and tail latency, not just average latency, determine whether a service meets its latency target or a control loop meets its deadline.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Deterministic execution is a commercial differentiator, especially for real-time and automotive uses.

insights.claim: Autoregressive decode often performs little computation per byte moved, particularly at low batch sizes, so performance depends more on memory bandwidth, capacity and data movement than on peak arithmetic throughput.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Memory bandwidth, not compute, is the binding constraint for LLM decode; supports HBM and memory-centric designs.

insights.claim: Not all inference is memory-bound: prefill can be compute-intensive with long inputs and large batches, while token-by-token decode is often bandwidth-limited.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Optimal hardware balance varies by phase, batch, sequence length and quantization; avoid one-size claims.

insights.claim: Most current models are too large for on-chip SRAM or cache, so parameters are fetched from high-bandwidth memory and sometimes across devices, and arithmetic units sit idle when data arrives too slowly.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Idle compute from memory starvation is the efficiency loss challengers target.
insights.locator: Most current models are too large

insights.claim: VSORA targets the memory wall with a compiler-directed architecture that exposes on-chip working memory as a single large register file implemented in SRAM, which compute can address with single-cycle throughput.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: A distinct architecture versus GPU cache hierarchies; the claim remains a company assertion.
insights.locator: VSORA's Architecture Targets the Memory Wall

insights.claim: Compiler-scheduled data placement instead of hardware-managed caches reduces timing variation from cache hits, misses and replacement, helping control tail latency.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Predictable latency is a selling point for real-time inference.

insights.claim: VSORA reports sustained utilization above 50% for LLM inference, but the article notes this depends on model, precision, batch size, sequence length and utilization definition, and needs independent matched-workload tests.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Treat the utilization claim as unverified until benchmarked independently.

insights.claim: VSORA's Matrix Processing Unit has a 16,384-bit-wide output datapath and runs AI, DSP and general-purpose code in vector or tensor mode within the same engine, and can run next-token sampling such as top-k without host transfers.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Fusing DSP and AI workloads suits edge and automotive systems that mix sensor processing with inference.

insights.claim: VSORA supports numerical formats from FP32 to FP4, with precision selectable per layer to match each layer's quantization tolerance.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Per-layer precision improves arithmetic density and memory use at preserved accuracy.

insights.claim: VSORA's two-stage flow exports PyTorch models to ONNX into a graph compiler that generates C++, then a modified LLVM backend produces a RISC-V application and MPU instructions.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Avoids CUDA lock-in in principle, but adoption depends on ONNX operator coverage and compiler quality.
insights.locator: VSORA's Compilation Flow and Software Stack

insights.claim: Without a hardware-managed cache hierarchy, the compiler carries more responsibility, so actual utilization depends heavily on generated code quality.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Compiler maturity is the key execution risk for the architecture.
insights.locator: Actual hardware utilization will therefore depend

insights.claim: VSORA's chiplets each hold two MPUs in two clusters, with a nominal 200 TFLOPS dense FP8 per MPU and 400 TFLOPS per chiplet, scalable by varying the compute chiplet to HBM3E stack ratio.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Modular ratio tuning lets one design address both compute-heavy and memory-heavy workloads.

insights.claim: VSORA's Jotunn8 combines eight compute chiplets with eight HBM3E stacks, specified at 288 GB of HBM and 3.2 PFLOPS peak dense FP8; these are rated peaks, not delivered performance.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Flagship data-center inference part to benchmark against GPU incumbents.

insights.claim: VSORA's Tyr family targets edge and automotive with two or four compute chiplets and one HBM3E stack, designed to meet ISO 26262 and ASIL functional-safety requirements.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Automotive inference silicon with safety targets is a niche beyond data centers.
insights.locator: The Tyr family is intended for edge applications

insights.claim: The author argues VSORA combines the predictable execution of SRAM-centered architectures with enough external memory for large models, distinguishing it from other inference accelerators.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: The positioning is promotional; competitive differentiation versus SRAM-centric rivals needs independent validation.
